messages.subject: Re: confused about geom_rect
parts:
I guess when it is trying to define the x and y axis it is using the a and b from the aes() call in the ggplot() call as reference, but when you then use a different data for your geom_rect() layer it doesn't know what to do. 

If you switch df2 and df1 like below the code works without error so it is clearly the lack of an a and b value in your df2 dataframe. That being said, geom_rect() does not require an x or y in the aes() call as you noted. It does seem slightly inconsistent but easily avoidable.

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)

ggplot(data = df2, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
               data = df1,

xmin = 0,
               xmax = 1,
               ymin = 0,
               ymax = 1)

I think the more important question would be why are you wanting to reference one dataframe and then supply geom_rect() another? If you have more than one dataframe to reference then you will likely have another layer to plot. Best thing to do is to supply each layer individually with "data=df, aes(x=x, y=y,...)" to avoid confusion for you and the program. 

HTH, 

Brandon

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: confused about geom_rect
parts: Hi:

On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 9:09 AM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
Can anyone tell me why this works:
==============================
df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
               xmin = 0,
               xmax = 1,
               ymin = 0,
               ymax = 1)
==============================

It works because you established a coordinate system for the plot by defining a for x and b for y relative to df1. Once that coordinate system is established, it can determine xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax because it has a reference system with which to work. Since you provided no new data frame, by default geom_rect() will refer to the coordinate system set up in the ggplot() call; specifically, the use of a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable.

but this doesn't (adding data parameter to geom_rect):
==============================
df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
               data = df2,
               xmin = 0,
               xmax = 1,
               ymin = 0,
               ymax = 1)
==============================

In this snippet, you defined a coordinate system using a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable in the first line with respect to df1. Consequently, ggplot() assumes that variables a and b correspond to the x and y variables in subsequent layers *unless explicitly overwritten*. Since a and b do not exist in df2, you get the error message as shown below. This is a common 'gotcha' in ggplot2 and is worth remembering when using multiple data frames to construct a plot...been there :)

*Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated...it takes a while to fully grasp this concept.

> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
+ geom_rect(
+               data = df2,
+               xmin = 0,
+               xmax = 1,
+               ymin = 0,
+               ymax = 1)
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found
To illustrate my point, this works:

ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
 geom_rect(
                data = df2,
aes(x = aa, y = bb),

xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = 1)

Notice the redefinition of x and y as aesthetics to conform to the variables in df2 not common to df1.

This also works:

df2 <- df1              # df2 now has same variables as df1

ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
                data = df2,
                xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = 1)
As does this:
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)

ggplot() + geom_rect(
                 data = df2,
                 aes(x = aa, y = bb),

xmin = 0,
                 xmax = 1,
                 ymin = 0,
                 ymax = 1)

This last approach is often useful if you know that you will be creating multiple layers in a plot using different variables with different names. Under this approach, all of the necessary aesthetics must be defined within the geom.

Disregard the fact that I'm not using the dataframes for anything in
my example. I plan to use them if I can.

Which is why I raised the last approach, in the hope it may come in handy for you...

Dennis

David

Hi:

On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 7:55 PM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thanks Dennis, that's very helpful.

In fact, I was assuming that "*Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated". In particular, I was assuming that since geom_rect needs an xmin and therefore also needs an x, it would look for it first in df2 (which it apparently does do) but then, not finding it, would look in df1, which it apparently does not do. So the statements are not very well coordinated, or at least in the way I was assuming.

So, here's my question: if I want to plot points in one layer and (positionally independent) rectangles in a different layer, what's the best way to set up two data frames for this?My approach was to put the coordinates for the points in one data frame (two for each) and the coordinates for the rectangles in the other (four for each), but that doesn't work.

When I confront this problem, and I have a few times, I try to define the coordinates of rectangles in terms of an established x-y coordinate system, which may require that I add variables to the data frame of the rectangle(s) corresponding to those that define the (x, y) aesthetics in the ggplot() call. I do that to minimize headache inducement and BP spikes.
 
By experimenting based on your tips, here's what I came up with:
df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1, c = c(1, 2), d = c(1, 2))

ggplot() +
geom_rect(
               data = df2,
               aes(

xmin = c - 1,
                       xmax = c + 1,
                       ymin = d - 1,
                       ymax = d + 1
               )
) +
geom_point(
               data = df1,
               aes(x = a, y = b),
               colour = "red"
)


Yes, but what did you define as the x and y aesthetics in geom_rect()? Nothing was set with the ggplot() call nor in the geom_rect() call. When the argument to ggplot() is empty, all aesthetics have to be mapped *within each geom*. You did that in your call, but the aesthetics defined in geom_rect() are relative to df2 whereas the aesthetics defined in geom_point() are relative to df1. If you hadn't put in the geom_point() code, ggplot() would have had to construct the axis and coordinate system from the information it had available, which would have been from (xmin, xmax) and (ymin, ymax).  [And it actually works - I tried it :-] If you look at the on-line help page of geom_rect(), you'll see that x and y are not required inputs per se....

Here's another example for your consideration:

df4 <- data.frame(g = c(1, 2), h = c(1, 2))

ggplot() +
    geom_rect(
               data = df2,
               aes(

xmin = c - 1,
                       xmax = c + 1,
                       ymin = d - 1,
                       ymax = d + 1
                    )
             )  +
    geom_point(data = df4,
                        aes(x = g, y = h),
                        color = 'red',
                        size = 3
                      )

There are neither variables named g and h in df2 nor variables named c and d in df4, and yet it works :)  Which geom establishes the coordinate system?

This works, but df2 is:

> df2
 a b c d
1 1 1 1 1
2 1 1 2 2

which means that the values of the a and b variables are meaningless. All they do is to signal geom_rect to use the same x and y as geom_point does.

The variables a and b in df2 are not meaningless, but they were never invoked into use in your geom_rect() example.

While this works, there must be a more sensible way to do this.


Happy New Year!!
Dennis

PS: Thank you for providing readable spacing and line breaks in your code. I hope it inspires others to try the same (hint! :)

David

> Which is why I raised the last approach, in the hope it may come in handy for you...

messages.subject: Re: confused about geom_rect
parts:
Geom rect neither requires nor uses x and y aesthetics, but if you
supply them they must exist. You could argue this is a bug, but it's a
pretty minor one.

Hadley

On Saturday, January 1, 2011, Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi:
>
> On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 7:55 PM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks Dennis, that's very helpful.
>
> In fact, I was assuming that "*Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated". In particular, I was assuming that since geom_rect needs an xmin and therefore also needs an x, it would look for it first in df2 (which it apparently does do) but then, not finding it, would look in df1, which it apparently does not do. So the statements are not very well coordinated, or at least in the way I was assuming.
>
> So, here's my question: if I want to plot points in one layer and (positionally independent) rectangles in a different layer, what's the best way to set up two data frames for this?My approach was to put the coordinates for the points in one data frame (two for each) and the coordinates for the rectangles in the other (four for each), but that doesn't work.
>
> When I confront this problem, and I have a few times, I try to define the coordinates of rectangles in terms of an established x-y coordinate system, which may require that I add variables to the data frame of the rectangle(s) corresponding to those that define the (x, y) aesthetics in the ggplot() call. I do that to minimize headache inducement and BP spikes.
>  By experimenting based on your tips, here's what I came up with:
>
> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
> df2 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1, c = c(1, 2), d = c(1, 2))
> ggplot() +
> geom_rect(
>                data = df2,
>                aes(
>                        xmin = c - 1,
>                        xmax = c + 1,
>                        ymin = d - 1,
>                        ymax = d + 1
>                )
> ) +
> geom_point(
>                data = df1,
>                aes(x = a, y = b),
>                colour = "red"
> )
>
>
> Yes, but what did you define as the x and y aesthetics in geom_rect()? Nothing was set with the ggplot() call nor in the geom_rect() call. When the argument to ggplot() is empty, all aesthetics have to be mapped *within each geom*. You did that in your call, but the aesthetics defined in geom_rect() are relative to df2 whereas the aesthetics defined in geom_point() are relative to df1. If you hadn't put in the geom_point() code, ggplot() would have had to construct the axis and coordinate system from the information it had available, which would have been from (xmin, xmax) and (ymin, ymax).  [And it actually works - I tried it :-] If you look at the on-line help page of geom_rect(), you'll see that x and y are not required inputs per se....
>
> Here's another example for your consideration:
>
> df4 <- data.frame(g = c(1, 2), h = c(1, 2))
>
> ggplot() +
>     geom_rect(
>                data = df2,
>                aes(
>                        xmin = c - 1,
>                        xmax = c + 1,
>                        ymin = d - 1,
>                        ymax = d + 1
>                     )
>              )  +
>     geom_point(data = df4,
>                         aes(x = g, y = h),
>                         color = 'red',
>                         size = 3
>                       )
>
> There are neither variables named g and h in df2 nor variables named c and d in df4, and yet it works :)  Which geom establishes the coordinate system?
>
> This works, but df2 is:
>
>> df2
>  a b c d
> 1 1 1 1 1
> 2 1 1 2 2
>
> which means that the values of the a and b variables are meaningless. All they do is to signal geom_rect to use the same x and y as geom_point does.
>
> The variables a and b in df2 are not meaningless, but they were never invoked into use in your geom_rect() example.
>
>
> While this works, there must be a more sensible way to do this.
>
>
> Happy New Year!!
> Dennis
>
> PS: Thank you for providing readable spacing and line breaks in your code. I hope it inspires others to try the same (hint! :)
>
>
> David
>
>
>> Hi:
>>
>> On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 9:09 AM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> Can anyone tell me why this works:
>> ==============================
>> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
>> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
>> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
>> geom_rect(
>>                xmin = 0,
>>                xmax = 1,
>>                ymin = 0,
>>                ymax = 1)
>> ==============================
>>
>> It works because you established a coordinate system for the plot by defining a for x and b for y relative to df1. Once that coordinate system is established, it can determine xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax because it has a reference system with which to work. Since you provided no new data frame, by default geom_rect() will refer to the coordinate system set up in the ggplot() call; specifically, the use of a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable.
>>
>> but this doesn't (adding data parameter to geom_rect):
>> ==============================
>> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
>> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
>> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
>> geom_rect(
>>                data = df2,
>>                xmin = 0,
>>                xmax = 1,
>>                ymin = 0,
>>                ymax = 1)
>> ==============================
>>
>> In this snippet, you defined a coordinate system using a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable in the first line with respect to df1. Consequently, ggplot() assumes that variables a and b correspond to the x and y variables in subsequent layers *unless explicitly overwritten*. Since a and b do not exist in df2, you get the error message as shown below. This is a common 'gotcha' in ggplot2 and is worth remembering when using multiple data frames to construct a plot...been there :)
>>
>> *Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated...it takes a while to fully grasp this concept.
>>
>> > ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
>> + geom_rect(
>> +               data = df2,
>> +               xmin = 0,
>> +               xmax = 1,
>> +               ymin = 0,
>> +               ymax = 1)
>> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found
>>
>> To illustrate my point, this works:
>>
>> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
>>  geom_rect(
>>                 data = df2,
>>                 aes(x = aa, y = bb),
>>                 xmin = 0,
>>                 xmax = 1,
>>                 ymin = 0,
>>                 ymax = 1)
>>
>> Notice the redefinition of x and y as aesthetics to conform to the variables in df2 not common to df1.
>>
>> This also works:
>>
>> df2 <- df1              # df2 now has same variables as df1
>> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
>> geom_rect(
>>                 data = df2,
>>                 xmin = 0,
>>                 xmax = 1,
>>                 ymin = 0,
>>                 ymax = 1)
>>
>>  As does this:
>> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
>> ggplot() + geom_rect(
>>                  data = df2,
>>                  aes(x = aa, y = bb),
>>                  xmin = 0,
>>                  xmax = 1,
>>                  ymin = 0,
>>                  ymax = 1)
>>
>> This last approach is often useful if you know that you will be creating multiple layers in a plot using different variables with different names. Under this approach, all of the necessary aesthetics must be defined within the geom.
>>
>>
>> Disregard the fact that I'm not using the dataframes for anything in
>> my example. I plan to use them if I can.
>>
>> Which is why I raised the last approach, in the hope it may come in handy for you...
>>
>> Dennis
